#2757. Den Questions: Finding Identity In Turmoil

Welcome back to the Den. The Wolves are ten games in and their record stands at 7-3. Over that time the Wolves sprinted out of the gates, lost Anthony Edwards to dirty knees in need of a cleaning, and have mostly righted the ship. Their losses are on travel back-to-backs and their first game without Edwards where they didn't even have a chance to practice before tip-off.

This team found something special in their first four games and then had their literal knees cut from them. Through the mire of the early season, as the rest of the league reels from their own injuries, the Wolves are looking for another new identity. An identity that does not include Edwards but prepares for his return.

As you can imagine, there are a lot of questions for this team to answer. Here are some of them.

Note: So much of this is small sample size theater.

It's just flashes. He had similar highs in Golden State before cooling down. There's no way he can keep this up. Here he goes again driving into traffic to get blocked… huh, nice pass. No no no, don't shoot tha…SPLASH! Oh my gawd, he got up so high for that rebound.

This short-staged drama has occurred inside my head in nearly every game this year. In good games and bad, Jonathan Kuminga has shown up to do whatever is asked of him.

In every counting stat except points per game, Kuminga is averaging career bests; rebounds (5.7), assists (2.9), steals (1.2) and blocks (1.0). His highest BPM through his first five seasons was 0.1. This season he is at 2.9 and has his career first positive for Offensive Box Plus Minus (0.6).

Head Coach Chris Finch has heaped praise on JK. In Minnesota's more read and react, flow, style, the Wolves starting power forward is emboldened to make a play when the ball finds him. His cuts aren't always rewarded but it sends the defense into a panic and opens things up for his teammates. It also puts him in the middle of the floor to grab or poke out offensive rebounds.

I am running out of excuses for why it won't last. After the first few games, I thought his play would disappear once the initial novelty of the season's start wore off. It didn't.

I thought he'd become more shot hungry and ball dominant when Ant went down. He hasn't.

I thought he'd get worn down having to guard some of the best players in the league night after night. This might happen as the overlong season grinds on, but so far Kuminga seems to get up for the battle.

The hardest question might be coming, "Can the Wolves afford to keep Kuminga?"

The start of the season has seen a dramatic drop in Rudy Gobert's points per game and his near league-best shooting efficiency. Gobert is averaging his fourth fewest shot attempts, second least points per game, the worst shooting percentage, and worst free throw percentage of his career.

It took one of the smartest basketball minds in Mike Conley over a year to learn how to play with Rudy. LaMelo Ball has had a scant few weeks to build chemistry. Combine that with the geometry of the floor and the defensive attention he is getting due to the sidelined Edwards, and it's no surprise the lack of consistency.

The Wolves need Rudy to be effective on offense. The book is out on the big man. Good defenses know how to bait Minnesota into thinking Rudy is open and recover quick enough to force a turnover or an errant shot.

Which brings us to the question of how to effectively use Gobert on offense. There is space to use him in the pick n' roll, but that has rarely been Finch's play style of choice. He is averaging a career high in offensive rebounds and this is primarily where I want him to find his points.

Finishing those misses just as they bounce off or tipping them out to teammates to try again when defenders are too close to him. Don't give them a chance to send him to the line.

He is very good at screening his teammates open and should continue to be used as the effective body in the way. This opens up Ball, Ayo Dosunmu, and Bones Hyland to get a screen assist into open triples. But this also pulls Rudy away from the hoop and the offensive boards that are his best offense.

Simple as it sounds his threat to roll is only as effective as his chemistry with his point guard. Until that firms up, he's on cleanup duty.

The Wolves are getting spooky with a lot more ghost screens this season. This gambit, that asks a shooting threat to feint a screen before sprinting to the other side of the point-of-attack (POA) defender, is meant to short circuit a defense. In a fraction of a second, the ghost screener's defender has to determine if they need to call for a switch if the screen gets set, or to chase after the shooter who has suddenly burst to a preferred place to spot up.

The Wolves are loaded with players who can quickly turn on the jets (I can't recommend Ayo Dosumnu's Player's Tribune piece enough) and make this decision that much harder. Screens are overcome best when a defense is communicating. The threat of a ghost screen shortens that window for effective communication.

If the POA defender thinks a screen is about to be set, they might get ready to hedge for the incoming contact giving the ball handler enough wiggle room to drive. If the chase defender thinks a screen is being set, they might slow up enough to give the ghost screener a chance to find an open look. If a screen is set, the game flows into common pick n' roll, one of the most tried and true means of creating advantages.

In the clip below, the Wolves use a combination of screens to break Orlando's zone, a past bugaboo for Minnesota.

Armed with better outside shooting than the past two years, look for the Wolves to continue to haunt perimeter defenders with these scary non-screens.

Note: Every injury to a player is unique. No timeline to return or level of ability when returning is the same. An Achilles tear for Donte DiVincenzo and his play style is a completely different injury that an Achilles tear for Ariel Hukporti and how he approaches the game, despite hurting the same tendon.

The day after it was announced that Ant would get arthroscopic knee surgery, a friend of mine sent me a grim text. All he could think of was Grant Hill, Brandon Roy, and Penny Hardaway and the possibility that Ant's career would be sapped from him like it had from those elite athletes.

I immediately texted back "What about DWade, Kobe, CP3?" After a brief internet search here are several NBA players who have undergone arthroscopic knee surgery who had some of their best years after the fact.

Kobe Bryant – Kobe had his first knee surgery in 2003, another in 2006, and another in 2010. In the midst of this string of surgeries he was an All-Star every year (despite the Laker bump, these were earned), won an MVP and was top five in MVP voting in all but one year, and made All-Defensive Teams in every year but one.

Dwyane Wade – DWade (a frequent Ant comp) had his entire left meniscus removed in 2002 while in college and went on to have a Hall of Fame career where he was unwillingly nicknamed Flash for how quick he was despite playing sans knee cartilage.

Chris Paul – Snitch Paul had arthroscopic knee surgery to repair a meniscus tear in 2010 while still with the New Orleans Hornets. As fun as he was on those Hornets teams, the Point God emerged into a force in the years after with the Lob City Clippers, Hardenball Rockets, and even made his first Finals with the Phoenix Suns, 11 years after the surgery.

Jimmy Butler – General Soreness had surgery on his right knee in 2018 while the Wolves were third in the Western Conference. He returned to help break the 14 year playoff drought. Jimmy has since been the driving force to two NBA finalist teams, never winning one. He adds multiple All-Star selection, an All-NBA selection, and an All-Defensive Team honor to his otherwise championship barren trophy case. I'm not bitter.

Jaylen Brown – Mr. Lamb Chops and Gravy had a knee procedure in the summer of 2025 and was back by training camp en route to being an All-Star, All-NBA 2nd Team, and sixth in MVP voting.

This surgery to clean up Ant's knee will likely diminish Ant's burst athleticism. He has moved his game to more outside shooting while maintaining a rim presence. If his downhill game is not as quick, it will hurt, but he's also added a midrange for if the defender goes too far under that leaves him a three level problem for any defense.

Plenty of NBA greats have bounced back, here's hoping Ant joins this laudable list.

Ant is out for roughly two months. Terrance Shannon Jr. has missed two games with a hip contusion. Donte DiVincenzo is recovering from an Achilles tear with every intention of coming back this season.

In their absence the Wolves have slotted Ayo Dosunmu into the starting lineup. Bones Hyland is scoring the ball well. Jaylen Clark is getting into guys jerseys and hitting 41.2% of his threes on 2.1 attempts a game.

All of these players are competing with each other for minutes. While the deeper bench has done yeomen's work to keep the Wolves head above water, they are not as good as the players whose minutes they are sopping up.

Finch is strict in his rotations. In the last three years, his starting lineups are in the top five for most used lineups in the NBA. If he gets a fully healthy team, Bones and Clark's minutes will likely disappear all together. Ayo will move back into his sixth man role ready to be whatever his team needs of him.

Donte is the biggest question mark. He started all 82 games last season, but there is not a spot for him in this starting lineup. We also don't know what he will look like coming back from such a devastating injury.

Sans LaMelo foul trouble giving Bones more minutes in the Raptors game, Finch has only given double digit minutes out to nine players before the injuries started. Joan Beringer's minutes aren't going anywhere. Trey Lyles has size, outside shooting, and has shown a predilection for being in the right place at the right time. Unless countering a specific lineup, his minutes stay the same.

Shannon figures to be the first cut in playtime with the Big Ragu's return unless Finch expands his bench to ten. And yet, there are few players who could elevate TJ's game better than Donte. An attacking TJ off a Beringer screen with Donte, Ayo, and Trey spreading the floor is tailormade to confound defenses.

On those nights where the injury report is blank, I hope Finch keeps the pedal to the metal with frequent rotations in the vein of Memphis Grizzlies coach Tuomas Iisalo. The Grizz have 13 players averaging double digit minutes and only two players over 30 minutes a game, Cameron Boozer (32.3) and Ty Jerome (30.7).

The NBA season is grueling. We have seen year after year the Wolves struggle as the playoffs wear on. TJ, Bones, and Clark are good players, deserving of minutes that will keep the starters fresh for when they are needed most.

Look here for the inarguable answers through the first ten games.

The Wolves are presently top five in the league in the following team categories:

The Net Rating stat is leaning heavily on Minnesota's first three blow out wins. That said, they have only lost their games by a combined 17 points thus far. They are hitting plenty of threes. They are defending with energy and diving for loose balls. They don't treat the game as something that should be handed to them like some legacy Ivy Leaguer applying at his dad's company. They are battling for the ball and snatching it from less hungry competition.

Gone are the days of XL T-Shirts and Howl Towels. The Wolves have overloaded this season with all manner of tchotchke, curio and baseball jersey to lure fans and collectors alike to home games. Most of these do not have an image released but give you just enough information to send your imagination whirring.

There is an entire series of baseball hats with design help from former Wolves vets. For Kevin Garnett's jersey retirement, Minnesota has five unique pieces of career spanning collectible celebrating the Big Ticket's accomplishments wearing 21. There are bobbleheads, blankets, and backpacks and way way way too many baseball jerseys. And here they all are, definitively ranked.

There are seven ticket package giveaways featuring a baseball jersey this season. In collaboration with local artists, this is what the Wolves are doing for their Artist's Series this year. Each jersey, for a sport different than the one it is honoring, celebrates a societal cross-section; Latino Noche, Military Appreciation, Native American Heritage, Pride Night, Asian American and Pacific Islander Night, Black Excellence, and Inspiring Women.

I think the designs are fun. Each one is a variation with pin stripes in a variety of colors. Some of them have designs on the sleeve nodding to the theme of the night. All of them have "Wolves Basketball" on the back. And all of them are baseball jerseys.

I love the Artist's series. I have purchased at least one shirt each of the last two seasons. I love that a local artist gets to put their stamp on the Wolves design. I love that several of the local artists are BIPOC and women creators. I love that they came in a variety of T-shirts, sweatshirts, and hats.

I just don't understand the thought process in making seven different baseball jerseys. I don't know enough about production costs, or textiles, so forgive my potentially ignorant question, but, wouldn't a jersey with two less sleeves of material be cheaper while closer to the topic at hand? Can they not do basketball jerseys because of some contractual stuff with Nike? WHY!?

All that said, I think the Native American design is my favorite and I might need to get one.

The giddy win streak to start the season, like those first marathon steps past gathered supporters, can make you feel invincible. Before you know it, you're running faster than you can sustain and its only mile two.

This is not to say that what we saw in the first three games is unsustainable, but with Ant out, the team is grasping for an identity while still playing fast and loose. LaMelo is trying to play aggressive defense and fouling like crazy.

The race is still young though. The stored ATP that let the Wolves sprint out of the gate may be spent, but they have years of experience and the benefits of youth. In the first full month of the season, they are searching for a pace they can maintain.

#2756. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2752. JJ Redick was pleased with ‘awesome’ season debut from Adou Thiero

One of the standouts of the early stages of the preseason was Adou Thiero, who looked to have built on a strong Summer League and was ready to be part of the Lakers' rotation.

However, an ill-timed injury halted Thiero's progress and kept him out of the opening weeks of the regular season. After some patience to allow swelling in his knee to go down, Thiero finally made his season debut in Friday's win over the Blazers and looked like he hadn't missed a beat from the preseason.

In only six minutes, Thiero's impact was felt as he tallied four points, four rebounds and two assists. After the game, head coach JJ Redick was asked about his performance and got rave reviews.

"I thought his first two defensive possessions, he made mistakes and then after that he was awesome," Redick said. "He literally did everything we asked him to do. He was great on the offensive glass. Even sometimes when we didn't necessarily get the possession, he was tapping the ball and crashing.

"I thought the read he made out of the short roll, I think they blitzed three times in the first half and two of those were against him. He makes the short roll and he gets the lob. I thought he played a great game and, defensively, he was really good in the second half."

Thiero came in late in the first quarter in the role previously held by Jarred Vanderbilt and immediately made an impact. Given his leaping ability, Thiero being the ball screener and roll man felt like an obvious fit.

The Blazers immediately tested him as they blitzed Luka Dončić, forcing Thiero to not just be in the right spot in the short roll, but then make a decision. He nailed both aspects, setting up Ziaire Williams for a dunk.

Shortly after, the Blazers opted for a more traditional pick-and-roll coverage. This time, Thiero rolled hard to the rim and caught the lob for an athletic finish.

"He did great," Walker Kessler said of Thiero. "Obviously, we value Adou a lot. He's a very physical player. Really talented, athletic player. I mean, that lob he caught is very, very impressive. He had a really good debut for the season."

Thiero's athleticism is unparalleled on the roster — and among the elites of the elite in the league as a whole — and offers the Lakers a different dynamic. Thiero as a screener and roller won't always work as it did on Friday, but his athleticism and activity level will continue to jump off the screen.

The Lakers' hope now is that he can stay healthy and start to stack positive performances in the regular season.

#2749. What's grown at Bayern - and is now making the difference

Beanies pulled over their heads, down jackets already slipped on, Joshua Kimmich high-fived his teammates at the final whistle. The faces of the Bayern players revealed the relief but also the exertion of this afternoon. Once more before the international break, the team gave it everything and got three points. Against opponents who once again asked plenty of questions of FCB.

Our FC Bayern triumphed 2-1 at 1. FSV Mainz 05, maintaining their lead in the Bundesliga standings. It wasn't a victory in which everything happened effortlessly. The hosts defended valiantly, looked for the duels and kept battling until the end. The fact the men from Munich still left as deserved winners is down to, one, the goals from Kimmich and Lennart Karl, and two, how naturally this team now combines technical quality with intensive effort.

"I'd call it a hard-earned victory. For the neutral it certainly wasn't a dazzling display, but still very confident," assessed Kimmich.

Anyone who wanted to understand why Bayern are still unbeaten in the Bundesliga after nine matchdays this season found answers in Mainz. The record champions circulated the ball with precision, moved with purpose and always searched for new passing channels. And if the ball was ever lost, the work to win it back began immediately from the front: with aggressive counter-pressing, short distances and great determination.

That was crucial, particularly against Mainz's compact back five. The hosts made the spaces tight and tried to break up Bayern's rhythm. "Mainz do the dirty things, they always go for the second balls, they're committed in the tackles – that doesn't make it easy. We stood up to that well," commented Aleksandar Pavlović. He and his colleagues accepted the challenge, without losing their style of play.

The numbers back that up: 68.8 percent possession, 717 passes played, of which an impressive 90.9 percent reached a teammate. In addition, 26 attempts on goal and 46 touches in the opposition penalty area. Stats that underline Bayern's dominance, but only tell part of the story.

"We're pleased that we won. We're a little disappointed to have conceded the goal at the end, but we know it's always a tough game here at Mainz. We had to suffer at times, but we were well prepared and stood our ground well," said assistant coach Aaron Danks, who again stood in for head coach Vincent Kompany, who is still recovering from illness.

That the Bavarians were able to convert their superiority into goals is thanks to two special moments. Kimmich put FCB in front with a delightful long-range shot from around 18 metres in the 14th minute, before Karl made it 2-0 in the 57th. Both goals were set up by Harry Kane.

The Ballon d'Or winner once again demonstrated that he's far more than a goalscorer for this team. With eight assists after nine matchdays, Kane has set a new record since detailed data collection began in 2004/05. At the same time, he's already equalled his personal best for one Bundesliga season.

That said, the game also highlighted where Bayern can still improve. Despite 26 attempts, nine shots on target and five big chances, they didn't manage to turn that dominance into a clearer scoreline. That meant Mainz remained in the game, even scored a potential equaliser – which was ruled out for offside – and did bring some renewed tension with a late goal. A reminder that even clear superiority in play is no guarantee for a comfortable win.

And another negative: captain Manuel Neuer was forced off, with Jonas Urbig replacing him between the posts.

The best photos from Bayern's Bundesliga game away at Mainz on Matchday 9 of the 2026/27 season.

When the players went over to their travelling fans after the final whistle, the relief was clear to see. The applause was deserved and the reward for passing a tough test before the forthcoming international break. After that, Bayern return to action against 1. FC Köln at the Allianz Arena (Matchplan).

"What's grown over the last two, three years is very special. There's great calmness at the club. You have the feeling that everything fits. We have to play successful football, that's the basis. But we've seen in the last few weeks that we stick together," summarised Kimmich.

What was Kimmich was describing was also discernible at the MEWA Arena on Saturday. And it's a good foundation for the challenges that lie ahead following the international break.

#2747. Early-season check-in on new Rockets Marcus Smart and Bogdan Bogdanovic

With the season being roughly one-tenth of the way through, I figured we could do a check-in on the two of the major offseason acquisitions, Bogdan Bogdanovic and Marcus Smart, who were signed to contracts paying them $3,524,115 and $6,064,00 this season, respectively.

Marcus Smart brings a lot more to the table for the Rockets than what appears in the box score. His defensive abilities, constant energy, and ability to make opposing guards miserable earned him Defensive Player of the Year honors in 2022. He brings another veteran presence to a young Rockets locker room. He will not be expected to score each night, but his ball-handling, shot creation, and the ability to make timely shots will make him a key piece of the Rockets' rotation.

So far this season, Marcus is averaging 9.8 points, 2.5 assists, 2.8 rebounds, and 1.3 steals while shooting 38.7% from three and 44.2% from the field. The field goal percentage is trending higher than his career average, as it three-point shooting, which is incredibly encouraging. Smart also had a stellar game vs. the Thunder, where he scored 24 points and made 7 three-pointers.

Houston needs perimeter shooting, and the 38% three-point shooter for his entire NBA career provides that. Bogdanovic can also create off the dribble at the second level of the offense and make shots when the main offensive players are on the bench or under heavy defensive pressure. He can create off the dribble at the second level of the offense and can make shots when the main offensive players are on the bench or under heavy pressure from the defense. This season, Bogdanovic is averaging 5.6 points per game, which does not seem like a lot, but he is shooting a blistering 45.5% from three. Any team can use that.

Bogdanovic is an excellent attacking addition to this year's sqaud. He can shoot, create off the dribble and space the floor, so he meets many of the Rockets' needs. However, his health and consistency will determine the effectiveness of this signing.

What is interesting about both of these acquisitions is the varying amounts of impact that each can bring to a game. Smart is brought in for his defense, energy, and leadership. Bogdanovic brings shooting, creation on offense, and floor spacing. Both players bring experience to Houston's young core and can help ease the transition of some of the young players into more rotation minutes as they continue to grow. They can be of use to players like Reed Sheppard by having veteran players on the team to help support the young players and to allow for more flexibility with lineups.

Ultimately, the value of both of these players will be determined by how they perform in games of consequence. Houston is trying to build a team of players that can help get them past the first round in the postseason, not just a collection of veterans and youngsters. If I had to give a grade for the two signings so far, I would give the Bogdonovic signing an A, and the Marcus Smart signing an A- only because Smart has missed time with an injury already.

Thats all for today! Make sure to let me know what you all think about the signings in the comments, and as always make sure to check back at The Dream Shake for all things Houston Rockets coverage.

#2744. Our 3 takeaways after Kansas State football's pathetic showing vs Oklahoma State

MANHATTAN — Kansas State didn't even put up a fight as it was trounced by Oklahoma State, as the Wildcats' first season under Collin Klein continues to fall apart.

K-State lost 66-28 to the Cowboys on Saturday, Nov. 7, at Bill Snyder Family Stadium. It was the Wildcats' third consecutive loss. The 66 points allowed were the sixth most in Wildcats history.

The Wildcats (4-5, 1-5 Big 12) had no answers for Oklahoma State's offense when it was rolling. At the same time, the offense was ineffective and turned the ball over three times.

Here are our immediate takeaways from the Wildcats' latest loss.

The Wildcats knew they had a tall task when going up against Oklahoma State's offense, which features quarterback Drew Mestemaker, who could be the No. 1 overall pick in the upcoming NFL Draft.

The Cowboys scored touchdowns on their first four drives. They had four touchdown drives that only took three plays, with three of them spanning 64 yards or more. Oklahoma State had never scored more than 45 points in Manhattan, and had 49 at halftime.

Mestemaker was great, finishing with 313 passing yards and four scores, along with one receiving and one rushing touchdown. Cowboys running back Caleb Hawkins rushed for 175 yards and three scores.

Barnett was presented with an opportunity against what's been a bad Oklahoma State defense. In a potential dress rehearsal to show that he can be a starting quarterback at the Power 4 level, he was benched at halftime.

Barnett was ineffective, completing 7 of 17 passes for 106 yards, a touchdown and one interception. His touchdown came on a 73-yard pass to a wide-open Derrick Salley, who didn't have anyone within 15 yards of him in apparent busted coverage. It's clearer than ever that the heir-apparent to Avery Johnson, whether that's next year or in 2028, is not on this roster.

Dillon Duff relieved him in the second half, after it was Barnett who relieved him the week before at Colorado. He looked more comfortable than he did against Colorado, but it was in garbage time and against backups.

K-State is trending toward an off-season where the phrase "roster overhaul" might not do it justice. Yes, Johnson's availability would have made a difference in the previous two games he missed, but the defense isn't close to competitive.

At this point, it would be surprising to see Kansas State win another game. TCU could lie down next week amid a disappointing season, but K-State could do the same. Arizona should be a big favorite in Manhattan on Nov. 21, while the Wildcats will likely be an underdog at Iowa State to close the year.

What a disappointing year Klein's first season looks like it will turn out to be. He'll have to consider many tough decisions after this season.

Wyatt D. Wheeler covers Kansas State athletics for the USA TODAY Network and Topeka Capital-Journal. You can follow him on X at @WyattWheeler_, contact him at 417-371-6987 or email him at wwheeler@usatodayco.com

The hosts end a three-game losing run in all competitions, while Gladbach's surprising unbeaten streak similarly ended after three matches. Polzin's men momentarily climbed seven places before the rest of matchday 9 action in Bundesliga.

#2740. Player Grades: Dallas gets on track against the Jazz with a 112-100 win

The Dallas Mavericks (5-4) took down the Utah Jazz (1-8), 112-100 on Friday night. The victory gets Dallas back on the right track after two-straight losses and gives the Mavs a 2-0 record in Emirates Cup play. Cooper Flagg and Kyrie Irving struggled a bit in the early going, but locked in down the stretch, while Morez Johnson, Jr. had the best game of his nascent NBA career.

We're switching it up this time and using a numerical grading system on a 10-point scale to grade the players. Let's get to the grades!

Irving was not sharp from the outset and had a difficult shooting night (7-of-20 overall; 0-of-3 from downtown). While that pulled down his grade, his all-out effort and hustle can't be overlooked. All night, Irving was on the floor lunging for steals, going amongst the trees for a couple of boards and hitting a few key shots in the latter part of the game to keep the Jazz at bay. It was not his best shooting night, but Irving made up for it in other ways, particularly on the defensive end.

Flagg shook off the massive funk he was in during the prior two games, but it took him until the second half to do so. He was 7-of-16 from the floor, with most of the misses coming in the first half and got completely lost on a couple of defensive sets, but he persisted. When it was all said and done, he nearly put up a triple-double. Three turnovers and 1-of-4 shooting from deep didn't help his grade, but this is the type of game that reminds you how special he is. He can have a rough half, yet end with a box score that looks great while having a true positive effect on the outcome of the game.

We try to show courtesy to all starters by featuring them in our Grades coverage, but Martin simply can't be graded. He missed a three-point attempt, committed two fouls and that's about it. He gets saved from an apparent 1/10 grade because he played so few minutes. Martin has been fine this year and contributes in ways that don't necessarily show in the box score, but one has to wonder if and when Zaccharie Risacher or Naji Marshall will start in his place.

Washington is like a new man this season, especially of late. He has played great ball and looks fully engaged over the past few games. It also appears as though he re-worked his shot in the offseason, to positive effect. Against Utah, Washington was 6-of-10 from downtown and led all players in scoring. If he can be a bit more consistent with this type of play, he will add another dimension to the team on both sides of the ball.

Gafford had a quirky game. His stat line doesn't blow you away and his single rebound is somewhat infuriating, however he only played 18 minutes. In that time, he was effective and did what the team needed him to do. His highlight was blocking a three-point attempt, picking up the rejected ball in stride and going in for a monster break-away slam to get the crowd into it.

If Clayton stays consistent, he is going to make Masai Ujiri, Mike Schmitz and Dusty May look like geniuses. On a team light on well-known guards, the Mavs front office picked up Clayton at the very start of the season and he's been great for his role. He shot only 1-of-5 from deep Friday night, but has been on fire from range to this part of the season and still managed to hit 50% of his eight shots overall. He's a capable player that can spell Irving and seeing him play well is no longer a surprise.

Johnson was an absolute beast. Compared to his first three games, Johnson looks like a different person. Whether it was shin splints early on or just acclimating to the NBA game, Johnson has experienced a major growth spurt. He is fouling less, playing better within the system and is much more explosive than he was early on. He was all over the boards, led the team in plus/minus with a +20 and was within the flow of the game throughout. This was a coming out party that was great to witness.

Dallas needed a win after getting smacked by the Kings and losing a close one to the Spurs. The Mavs couldn't sleep on the single-win Jazz (who are probably better than their record) like they did with the Kings. It appears they learned from that experience and played through some struggles to pull away. This also gives them their second Emirates Cup win in as many tries, while boosting their point differential as well.

I invite you to follow me @_80MPH on X, and check back often at Mavs Moneyball for all the latest on the Dallas Mavericks.

#2739. Brewers bash champion Dodgers to brink of NLCS sweep; CBS Sports Preseason All-America team revealed

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2738. Kansas State report card: Grading the Wildcats' flop vs Oklahoma State

MANHATTAN — The downfall of Collin Klein's first season as Kansas State's football coach hit its latest low point in its 66-28 loss to Oklahoma State.

The Wildcats didn't stand a chance. The Cowboys' high-powered offense got what it wanted, and the Wildcats' offense turned the ball over too many times to make it a shootout.

You can probably guess how our grades for this game turned out.

It doesn't matter that Kansas State played backup quarterbacks; the Wildcats should have played better against what's been a mediocre Oklahoma State defense. Everything was bad outside of the two times when the Cowboys forgot to cover Derrick Salley.

You can't give up 66 points and not get a failing grade, even if you forced a pair of turnovers.

At least they didn't allow Oklahoma State to return a punt for a touchdown? The hold on a good kickoff return to start the game set the tone. At least Monterrio Elston looks like a solid choice to return kicks.

You can't blame folks for questioning Jordan Peterson as the Wildcats' defensive coordinator. Collin Klein's offense had no answer for

Bartley had an interception and almost had a second.

If you were wondering, and I was, the NHL record for longest winless streak to start a season is 15 in a row by the 1943-44 New York Rangers. They lost 11 straight, tied a game, then lost three more before knocking off the visiting Boston Bruins.

So the Kings (0-4-2) have a long way to get there and haven't even tied the franchise record yet, as the 1984-85 club was winless in its first nine. L.A. still made the playoffs that year. This year's club is still priced +100 for extra hockey with No only slightly favored at -125. The updated season points total is 90.5 – remember, 84 regular-season games now. The Kings' preseason points total was 95.5, so the sportsbooks haven't given up on them yet, nor should they. Still too talented of a roster.

The goaltending has been problem No. 1, with the duo of Darcy Kuemper and Anton Forsberg combining for a 4.17 goals-against average that is third-worst in the NHL and an .861 save percentage that is second-to-last. The penalty kill ranks 31st at 61.9%. Perhaps a trade for Winnipeg holdout Connor Hellebuyck?

But the offense needs help too, putting up just 2.00 goals per game (31st) and converting 14.3% of the time on the power play (26th). L.A. scored eight total goals in its first two games and has scored exactly one in the next four. That's hard to do.

Injuries haven't helped, with the likes of Kevin Fiala, Alex Turcotte and Mats Zuccarello all on injured reserve. Coach Peter Laviolette said that Zuccarello is "trending" toward playing tonight, however, after practicing Monday on a line with center Quinton Byfield and Trevor Moore. No one has more than five points, and only three guys have a positive rating (all at plus-1).

"I'm not seeing [the lapses] from our fourth-line type players, I'm seeing it from our top players," All-Star defenseman and team captain Drew Doughty said over the weekend. "That's why we're losing games. Your top players need to be your best players every night and not just have flashes of brilliance. They need to play 60 minutes."

We should note that the Kings started 1-3-2 last season ahead of a long trip as similar to starts tonight, and they still managed to sneak into the playoffs, although they were then swept by Colorado. But I sure don't see any sure-fire wins on this five-game roadie. It likely will be Kuemper tonight, and in two road starts he has allowed 10 goals on 61 shots.

#2735. Crown Jewel 2026 takeaways: WWE has an Oba Femi problem, and Roman Reigns is caught in the middle

WWE Crown Jewel 2026 went down Saturday at the ANB Arena in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, after weeks of questions over whether the event would actually take place. Roman Reigns and Chelsea Green won their respective Crown Jewel Championship matches, Tiffany Stratton cashed in her Money in the Bank briefcase on Green to claim the Women's World Championship, Oba Femi helped Penta and Je'Von Evans win the WWE World Tag Team titles, and Cody Rhodes defeated Randy Orton in a Last Man Standing match.

As we regroup before Survivor Series: WarGames in a few weeks, here's four big takeaways from Saturday's action in Saudi.

WWE's intention of keeping the spotlight on Oba Femi is borderline exhausting at this point.

It's clear he's WWE's next big star and they've done everything they can to ensure he's front and center as often as possible. The problem with much of the "Raw" scene over on Monday nights is that it's littered with guys WWE is actively trying to build up. So in positioning Femi as the next big star, he's just constantly hammering down on talents who haven't quite made it yet (see: Bron Breakker, Bronson Reed, etc) versus if he was on "SmackDown," where he'd be punching up at established veterans.

That was the case on Saturday yet again, where Femi was the difference-maker in Je'Von Evans getting his first taste of WWE gold alongside the men's Money in the Bank briefcase holder, Penta, by slamming Reed off the entrance ramp. For Evans, it's another step forward in establishing himself on the upper echelon of the "Raw" roster, while Penta bides his time with the briefcase with a pinfall victory over Austin Theory.

Absent the tag-team championship, it'll be interesting to see how Bron Breakker navigates the next steps in his career. He exploded back from injury, seemed well-positioned to claim a world championship, and has really coasted most of this year. His placement in a next big thing vs. next big thing match with Femi earlier this year was perhaps the highlight of his year, alongside a win over Seth Rollins. He still just hasn't found his footing though, and he runs the risk of following a similar path Jacob Fatu endured this year in climbing the ranks before empty booking brought him back to Earth.

The odds weren't great for Sami Zayn to leave Saturday's main event with a win, and Roman Reigns ultimately closed the door on any chance of that happening with a spear.

Despite the loss, this match at least did more to establish Zayn as a legitimate champion, following the old "sometimes losing is winning" trope. Zayn pushed Reigns to his limits before inevitably falling short, and received a respectful hug from the World Heavyweight Champion before exiting the ring. But no matter the offense Zayn pulled out in this one — and he did appear close at times to earning the win — it was written in the stars that he'd be on the losing end.

Zayn and Reigns picked up from their rivalry years ago in a really strong build to their showdown, but there's almost no question how the next six months should pan out. Reigns' sole purpose is to look as strong as humanly possible before dropping the title to Oba Femi at WrestleMania next year. Until April of next year, it's hard to imagine any challenger putting a real test to "The Tribal Chief."

That being said, Saturday's main event is another example of how, Femi, the champion in waiting, puts a serious gridlock on the title picture (and every Reigns match, for that matter) in a similar way WWE has notoriously fallen for, whether it was Cody Rhodes waiting a year to beat Reigns or one of the John Cena-The Rock WrestleMania tilts.

It makes Reigns champion by default and removes any elements of surprise that made wins like Zayn's world championship victories so spectacular. When you remove the surprise factor in wrestling, it becomes your favorite show that mailed it in for half the year, absent almost any creativity. A Zayn loss also robbed fans of capitalizing on one of the best character developments in recent WWE television, making him even more insufferable than he already is. The finish line can still be the finish line, but what happens between now and then is one of the flattest lines WWE has drawn in some time.

Saturday's entire women's Crown Jewel match balanced between Liv Morgan being the proven, cocky champion, and Chelsea Green still working to prove she belonged despite having held the Women's World title since Money in the Bank. The formulaic approach panned out to a logical conclusion, after Morgan dismissed the Judgement Day and got caught in a roll-up to fall just short of the Women's Crown Jewel Championship.

As soon as Green got on the mic post-match, you just knew she'd be in trouble — and sure enough, Morgan's attack from behind set up a series of unfortunate events.

The perfect cherry on top was Tiffany Stratton hitting the ring and turning her back on Green with a briefcase hit to the head, forcing the champ to lose her title to a successful Money in the Bank cash-in.

Heel Stratton is perfect for "SmackDown" after incessantly trying to cash in her briefcase on Morgan to no avail. In a best-case scenario, the next month or so projects to follow Green playing a similar role as she did during Saturday's match, and proving she absolutely belongs in the title picture.

The story that's followed Cody Rhodes and Randy Orton since WrestleMania has been him pulling the trigger on punting his former mentor. Saturday's match was as brutal as expected, with intensity to open the bout and weapons quickly entering the fray.

Rhodes finished off Orton with a few Cross Rhodes — causing Orton's head to slam into the stairs — followed by the punt kick to keep the former world champ on the mat for the 10-count. The final sequence culminated months of build-up to the very moment Rhodes' foot slammed into Orton's head, and should now signal the end to their blood feud.

With the rest of the men's division essentially paired off, it'll be fascinating to see how Orton and Rhodes navigate their next steps.

For Rhodes, a return to the title picture seems like a logical path forward. He's sort of hovered right on the outskirts, occasionally finding his way into title matches since dropping the belt. But a fully-focused Rhodes promo about reclaiming his championship, while simultaneously competing in the upcoming John Cena Classic wouldn't be surprising.

With Orton unable to get back to his feet, there's less certainty about where he pops up next. My guess is he takes some time to heal before mixing it up with someone like Trick Williams.

#2734. NHL Power Rankings: Bruins, Jeremy Swayman off to a roaring start in a tough Atlantic Division

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

You can't make the playoffs in 10 games, but you can definitely give yourself some breathing room when the inevitable ebbs and flows of the season strike. That's exactly what the Boston Bruins have done as they've stood out for the right reasons in a deep Atlantic Division.

Boston currently leads the division with 15 points, and while the Tampa Bay Lightning's record is technically better, the Bruins' plus-14 goal differential is tied for second in the NHL.

The biggest reason for this fast start has been the play of Jeremy Swayman in goal. He's allowed one or fewer goals in half of his starts, and Swayman's 8.02 goals saved above average ranks second to old Beantown running mate Linus Ullmark, per Natural Stat Trick.

We have a long way to go before we start discussing Vezina Trophy candidates seriously, but Swayman certainly has the potential to carry Boston to the postseason.

It helps that David Pastrnak is an elite playmaker, and the Bruins have been getting contributions from young forwards Fraser Minten and James Hagens. Morgan Geekie has also gone from goal-scoring machine to distributor with seven assists in 10 games.

The Atlantic Division will be a heavyweight brawl throughout the season, but to this point, the Bruins have proven to be a worthy combatant. With that in mind, here are the updated NHL Power Rankings.
